title: Please… Enough with the Sloppy, One-Shot SaaS Replacements — Mahmoud Abdelwahab, Railway

when you could just do it yourself? Just

there's one missing piece that rarely
gets mentioned. And it's the fact that
there's a gap, a big gap between working
software that got oneshotted and
software I would actually use. Software

use. The tool allows us to manage
content for the Railway website, change

media. There's even a mini CRM so that
when we're working with like external

because you know you want to coordinate
multiple things and when they'll go out.

there's like comments, realtime editing
and it's all built using agents. I would

when you're a user, there's like a lot

patterns that I found that agents don't
typically do unless you explicitly ask
them to. And this is my list. So we'll
go through them one by one. And the
first one is like autosave. I found that
if like let's say I'm building some form
of document editor, autosave is kind of
like a table stakes feature. So rather
than manually clicking save to save
things, you just ask it to automatically
save progress in the background and to
make sure that it's like a non-blocking

one other kind of like step further that

>> just 700 million tokens later, I had

this is the first thing that I find

experience perspective. Another pattern
I found that agents completely forget to
implement is optimistic updates. So
rather than showing your users a bunch
of loading spinner whenever they're
taking any action, you essentially show
them the success state you know
optimistically
and in the background you're going to
sync whatever change they made. Now if
the sync or the operation fails for
whatever reason you just roll it back
and then tell them like oh the operation
work. Now of course you shouldn't
blindly have optimistic updates for
everything. There are some scenarios
where you want to show the user a
loading spinner and you're going to wait
to check that everything worked
properly. But in general, having
optimistic updates makes the overall
experience feel significantly faster,
much snappier, and it will just feel
much more instant. So pretty sure you
can just ask your agent like, "Hey, I
would like to implement optimistic
updates where it makes sense. Let's come
up with a plan." And it will tell you
all the areas where it makes sense to
do. Again, it's like it's not difficult
for the agent to build it. You just need
to ask and know exactly what to ask for.
Now, an extension of optimistic updates,
in my opinion, is giving users the
ability to undo certain actions. Now,
for example, if you ask your agent to
implement the ability to delete records,
what it will typically do is it will
give you a delete button. You click it,
might show a confirmation dialogue, you
hit confirm, and then it will actually
do the deletion. But a much nicer
experience is actually allowing the user
to undo that action. So they hit delete,
you immediately remove the item they
want to delete from the UI, but you tell
them like, hey, you have like a couple
of seconds where you could change your
mind. And if they don't do anything,
that means you actually want to delete a
thing. Then you actually implement the
operation. Otherwise, if they hit undo,
you just bring back the change. So it's
kind of like you do the operation in the
background as well. It's just kind of a
delayed action which kind of ties into
the next point which is archiving. You
should tell your agent you want the
ability to archive records and be able
to unarchive them because sometimes you
want to hide something from the UI
completely or let's say from search
results and archiving will be the way to
do it and you shouldn't force your user
to be like well if you don't want to see
this you have to delete it. and a much
better experience is just the ability to
walk out records. So I think it is a
pattern that should definitely exist.
Another big one for me is URL state. you
should ask your agent to persist in the
URL whenever it makes sense of course
and it's so useful because whenever you

conditions maintaining these things in

every day I think it makes a huge

that made the output significantly
better is telling the agent explicitly
to use existing pages as references when

how it works works and how the thing is
overall structured and that made it
possible for me to essentially define
what good looks like once and then just

follow it. I don't know if models like

that my success rate is higher whenever
I tell the agent to like, well, use an

lists of records that you can create
update and delete and like list well

you have opinions about something they

then this way your agent whenever it's
building something it will actually
follow those skills pretty closely. And
as I was building all of our internal
tooling, I found myself reaching for
three Asian skills. Uh two of them are

like better error messages in general.

for the agent to effectively work with
